extracted.intended_audience: mathematical teachers, advanced students, and geometers
extracted.subtask_short: series expansion and classical geometry methods
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological principles for performing formal series expansions (method of conditional coefficients, binomial, logarithmic, exponential series) and for analytic geometry problems (intersection of conics, sphere tangent to four spheres). Emphasises correct hypotheses, choice of expansions (ascending/descending), treatment of remainders and multi-valued roots, and systematic elimination procedures in geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and scope of the method of conditional coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of conditional (indeterminate) coefficients is a general instrument by which the expansion of individual functions and literal formulae for broad classes of functions (binomial, multinomial, exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric, Taylor series) may be obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confine the method to numerical approximation; treat it as a tool to deduce relations among coefficients (the 'scale of relation'). If desired, the remainder (value of omitted terms) can also be sought by this method and will agree with the result from algebraic division. The method is especially valuable for deriving general expansion formulae rather than isolated numerical values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal expansion from numerical applicability (convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal development (relation among coefficients) may be correct even when numerical application is impossible because of divergence or out-of-range arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying a formal series for numerical computation, check convergence conditions (e.g., magnitude relations like |x|<|a|). Do not conflate truth of the algebraic/formal development with its numerical validity; explicitly verify the domain where the expansion is meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose ascending or descending powers based on magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function is symmetric in two quantities, it can be developed in ascending powers of one and descending powers of the other; one expansion will converge where the other diverges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For numerical use, select ascending powers when the second term is smaller than the first, and descending powers when it is larger. Each expansion is inapplicable where the other is applicable; pick the form adapted to the numerical region of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial theorem with fractional indices — required transformations and sign care
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the binomial theorem to fractional indices tacitly involves hypotheses about which term is the 'second' (smaller) and the signs involved; neglecting this leads to incorrect expansions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always transform the expression so the development is in ascending powers of the second term (or equivalently avoid fractional indices in intermediate steps). When both signs are positive or when handling (β − a)^ν, rewrite to place the smaller term second (e.g., factor out a) so fractional indices are handled without fractional intermediate indices. Track double signs (a factor of (−1)^ν when needed) and change signs of odd powers of the second term as indicated. Use the recommended computational layout (numerical work method from Hutton) to reduce errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid neglecting multiple-valuedness for fractional exponents
rubrics_metrics.description: For expressions like a^{1/v} or (−a)^{1/v}, the expansion's reality or imaginariness depends on the chosen branch; fractional exponents produce multiple roots (v roots of ±1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that a^x for fractional x has multiple (v) values; expansions correspond to ordinary series multiplied by appropriate roots of unity. Determine whether the expansion is real or imaginary by examining the successive values and the parity of denominators; do not assume a single real value without checking branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logarithmic/exponential expansions require branch/argument consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying series for logarithms or exponentials to negative arguments leads to extra terms (e.g., log(−1)) and hence imaginary contributions; naive application gives inconsistent (infinite negative) results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When x solves a^x = −N, write x = log N + log(−1) (or analogous base changes) to account for imaginary parts. Always account for the complex logarithm when the argument is negative; do not use the positive-argument series blindly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovering remainders when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the method of conditional coefficients typically yields relations among successive coefficients, one can also obtain expressions (or bounds) for the remainder if that is made an explicit objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the remainder is required, pursue it via the same coefficient method (multiplying truncated series and equating coefficients, possibly reducing to a common denominator) — this can deliver the same general correction as algebraic division, though possibly with more algebraic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore congruity by forcing coefficients of incongruous powers to zero
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure expressions are congruous (consistent) under all circumstances, the coefficients of incongruous powers that would otherwise make results depend on incompatible assumptions must be separately and simultaneously set to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When different powers (e.g., arising from different branches or incongruous terms) must agree, impose zero conditions on the coefficients of those incongruous terms to obtain universally valid relations (example: solving binomial surd equations where rational hypotheses force certain coefficient equalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination procedure for intersection of two second-degree curves
rubrics_metrics.description: To find coordinates of intersection points of two conics, eliminate one variable to obtain a biquadratic equation in the remaining variable, from which up to four intersection points follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write each conic, manipulate into forms with coefficients as functions of the remaining variable, multiply suitable linear combinations (e.g., multiply (3) by a2 and (4) by a1 and subtract), introduce intermediate symbols (h_i,k_i,p,q etc.) for clarity, and eliminate y by forming resulting polynomial (see equations (8)–(13) and the final biquadratic). Use symmetry to obtain the analogous equation for the other variable. Special-case simplifications (centered curves, absence of linear terms, or degeneration to straight lines) reduce degree and simplify computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and exploit special/simpler cases in conic intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain coefficients vanish (e.g., linear terms absent, or second-power coefficients absent), the elimination simplifies: centered conics lead to quadratic forms; vanishing second-power coefficients reduce a conic to a straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check coefficient values early to simplify algebra: if linear terms are absent, set origin at common center and use reduced quadratic forms (equations (15),(16),(17),(18)). If second-degree coefficients vanish, treat as straight-line intersections (use simplified equations (19)–(21)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate transformation and discriminant analysis for circle vs central curve intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: When intersecting a circle with a central conic (ellipse/hyperbola), rewrite coefficients using compact notation (Q,R,H,K) and derive resultant quadratic/biquadratic formulas for coordinates; examine the radical's sign to determine contact, intersection, or no intersection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt standardized substitutions to reduce algebra (use Davies/Hutton notation). Compute the expressions under radicals in solution formulas: if zero, circle touches curve (tangency); if negative, no real intersection; if positive, four or two real intersections as indicated by geometry (pairs on diameters when symmetric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic reduction for sphere tangent to four given spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: Place coordinate origin and axes conveniently (e.g., at one centre, axis along line through two centres), write pairwise contact distance equations, subtract and divide sums to obtain symmetric linear/quadratic relations for coordinates and radii, and introduce reciprocal/normalized quantities to simplify the final algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the last four contact equations to determine relative coordinates; exploit symmetry to map solutions between analogous groups (change of radius positions). Subtract appropriate combinations ((3) from (1)+(2), etc.), divide by 2 to get symmetric linear equations (11)–(16), then derive relations (20)–(28) and introduce normalized reciprocals (s,p etc.) for further simplification (29)–(33). Solve resulting algebraic equations (including extracting square roots) to obtain centre coordinates and radius. To get the internally tangent sphere, replace sums of radii by differences in the same formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal-radius theorem for spheres tangent to four mutual-contact spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: When four spheres are placed in mutual contact and two spheres are described tangent to all four (one internally, one externally), there is an elegant reciprocal relation among their radii: the reciprocal of the least (inscribed) radius equals the sum of the reciprocals of the other five (after appropriate sign choices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use derived formulae (equations (37),(38)) and their subtraction/product to verify and apply the theorem. This reciprocal relation can serve as a check on algebraic solutions of the tangency problem.
